Muse Ember delivers more intelligence per dollar than Claude Haiku 5.5 or GPT-6 Luna at any reasoning setting: it matches Haiku's best score at about a third of the cost and beats every Luna setting. It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task.

Safety

Before release, we evaluated Muse Ember under our Meta Superintelligence Scaling Framework, including chemical and biological, cybersecurity, and loss-of-control risks. Across the categories assessed, our evaluations found that Muse Ember remained below the framework’s high-risk thresholds. Though it’s a small model, it received the same core safety training and testing. We also evaluated how Muse Ember behaves when acting on users' behalf. That covers whether it respects user intent, handles sensitive information appropriately, resists instructions hidden in web pages, documents, or tool outputs that try to redirect it, and seeks human input before high-impact actions.

Availability

Muse Ember is available today on Muse Code and Meta Model API as muse-ember-1.0. It costs $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.004 per million cached input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, with a 1M-token context window and up to 512K output tokens. Muse Ember supports the Responses API.

When we introduced Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, we said we would use them to develop specialized models we can bring to everyone. Muse Ember is the first trained using Muse Wonder Full. It rounds out our portfolio of models: Muse Wonder for the hardest problems, Muse Spark for coding and agentic workflows, and Muse Ember for repeatable coding and agentic tasks at scale at about $0.14 per Artificial Analysis task, a cost low enough to run in every product, for everyone.

entry.title: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2
entry.content:
We’ve upgraded Claude Fable and Claude Mythos—models that are designed to tackle the most daunting technical challenges.

Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision. During prerelease testing they’ve helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours—among many other applications we’ll discuss below.

Claude Fable and Claude Mythos are the same underlying model. Fable has strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards to guard against misuse, which allows us to make it available to all users. Organizations pursuing beneficial applications in cybersecurity or biomedical research can apply for access to Mythos through our recently expanded Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs.

Testers have found that Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 communicate more clearly than past Fable and Mythos models. They generate outputs up to 30% faster than Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, and they’re available at a lower price: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.

Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 also come with an optional fast mode, which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times. Fast mode is available for $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens.

Safety and alignment. To help ensure safety and alignment keep step with growing model capabilities, we ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes. We believe high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures. Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks.

We describe more about our safety testing below, and full details can be found in the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card.

When to use Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. Fable and Mythos are best for the most ambitious, open-ended technical work. For most coding and knowledge tasks, we recommend that users start with Claude Opus 5.5, our strongest daily driver, and then switch to a different model as required, depending on the scope and complexity of their work—upward to Fable or Mythos, or downward to Claude Sonnet 5.5 or Claude Haiku 5.5. Fable 5.2 can also play the role of Advisor (where Haiku, Sonnet, or Opus models consult it to help solve harder problems) or Orchestrator (where it delegates simpler tasks to smaller models).

Evaluating Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2

Effort and efficiency. On Medium effort (the default in Claude apps and Claude Code), Fable 5.2 can accomplish challenging tasks with fewer tokens than Fable 5.1. In early testing on the FrontierCode 2.0 evaluation, Fable 5.2 at High effort scored about level with Opus 5.5 at Max effort, for roughly half the cost per task. At Xhigh effort, it also scored the highest of any released model tested.

Coding

Over 90% of the changes merged into Anthropic’s core codebase are now written by Claude (with human guidance). We’ve used Fable 5.2 to fix stubborn bugs in minutes, optimize performance across all of our services, and complete high-value software projects that would otherwise have been too slow or too costly to attempt. A team of agents running an earlier version of Fable 5.2 migrated a critical production service from Python to Rust—the service is now more efficient, more reliable, and starts about 26 times faster. We’ve found that Fable 5.2 exercises strong engineering judgment and can produce high-quality results from even ambiguous requests.

As an experiment, one Anthropic engineer gave Fable 5.2 the task of designing a prototype operating system. Starting from an empty folder, the model coordinated over 1,000 subagents, working around the clock for eight days writing, testing, and reviewing code. It produced a working operating system that boots on a laptop, with its own core that runs the machine, drivers for the disk, keyboard, and network, permanent file storage, windows, a login screen, an installer, and built-in Claude functionality (see the video below).

Early testers have been impressed at how successfully Fable 5.2’s coding skills can be applied to a wide range of tasks:

Cybersecurity

Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity engineering. It catches more vulnerabilities than our previous models, and is better at reproducing and fixing them (note that Claude Fable 5.2’s safeguards will block most cybersecurity-related tasks). A security company found that one in six confirmed bugs found by Claude Mythos 5.2 were missed by all of the other frontier models they tested. On our internal evaluation, CVE Rediscovery,¹ Claude Mythos 5.2 found 10.2% more vulnerabilities than Claude Opus 5.5 and 14.4% more than Claude Mythos 5.1. Claude Mythos 5.2 also shows better judgment and calibration—one tester found that previous models had overstated the seriousness of about 1 in 20 findings, whereas Claude Mythos 5.2 hadn’t overstated any.²

Claude Mythos 5.2’s cyber capabilities are accessible through our Cyber Verification Program, which we’re continuing to expand and improve. Claude Enterprise customers (even if they aren’t members of the Cyber Verification Program) can access Claude Security, which scans codebases for vulnerabilities using our most capable models—which now includes Claude Mythos 5.2. A recent update to Claude Security helps it watch repositories as code is updated, track any findings to ensure they’re fixed, learn from additional context, and connect to a user’s tools through an API and MCP.

Science and engineering

Important tasks in science, engineering, and mathematics increasingly depend on coding: analyzing data, modeling molecules, designing parts, and controlling instruments are all done through software. Below, we discuss how Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 have helped researchers make progress on difficult problems in these areas.

Theoretical physics

Claude Fable 5.2 solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes, and the effort to unite the two linchpin theories of modern physics, relativity, and quantum mechanics.

Both of Claude’s results rely on holographic duality, the idea that certain universes containing gravity can be precisely described by a quantum theory containing no gravity at all. In the first problem, physicists in 1983 had shown that as these universes heat up, black holes form abruptly, like water boiling; but their method worked only in large universes that were big enough for relativity to apply. A calculation to determine whether the same was true in very small universes, where only the quantum description can be used, was laid out in 2003 but was too laborious to complete. Fable 5.2, working largely autonomously, completed it and found the transition is abrupt there, too. In the second problem, Fable 5.2 found the exact limit of a technique physicists have used for more than 15 years to rule out candidate theories of quantum gravity in a simplified universe. Read more about these results in their respective preprints, here and here.

Protein folding

Adeno-associated viruses are small, harmless viruses whose protein shell, the capsid, can be used to deliver gene therapies. The protein structure of the capsid is important—for example, it affects whether the therapy will be blocked by a patient’s immune system—but it’s also highly complex. Existing protein-folding models like AlphaFold can predict individual proteins, but a capsid is built from dozens of them. Building on two open-source protein-folding models, Claude Mythos 5.2 found a novel way to accurately predict a whole capsid’s structure. It wrote code that ran these models on overlapping groups of protein chains, and used the information on the known symmetries of the capsid to merge them together.

Claude’s method worked across several capsids, both natural and engineered (in our tests, it accurately modeled 28 of the 34 it attempted).³ Three computational biologists shared the following reflections on how Claude’s skills could be used to speed up their research into gene therapies:

Mathematics

Mathematical formalization. Formalization is the process of translating a mathematical proof into a language that a computer can check step by step. It can help human mathematicians gain confidence in results without having to check them by hand (this matters even more when AI models generate results that are hard for humans to verify). Because formalization is such a laborious process, if AI could assist with it, mathematicians could spend more time exploring novel ideas.

Our first formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem, performed by an unreleased research version of Claude, took 11 days. It relied on a purpose-built harness along with guidance from a human researcher. By contrast, a team of 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents fully formalized the theorem in just 30 hours, with minimal human intervention. Fable 5.2 started from minimal prompts, built its own ways to coordinate, and used no mathematical references, only a list of intermediate theorem statements to score progress. It needed one-third as many action tokens as our first formalization and produced a proof seven times shorter. As can be seen in the figure below, Opus 5.5 (with the same 1,000-agent setup) completed only 26% of the formalization in 18 hours, and barely made any more progress after 30.

Read more about the formalization here.

Hardware and robotics

Many of AI’s potential benefits—for example, in speeding up laboratory research—depend on it being able to act in the physical world. Claude Fable 5.2 continues our models’ trend of increasing usefulness in the real world, showing promising results on tasks such as designing hardware devices and substantial advances in controlling physical robots.

Hardware engineering. We tested Fable 5.2’s skills in hardware engineering, asking it in a one-paragraph prompt to design and produce three working electronic devices with their own circuit boards, 3D-printed enclosures, and software. The devices, shown below, were a home voice-assistant hub, a USB speakerphone, and a handheld virtual pet. We collaborated on this project with Diode, a company that designs and manufactures circuit boards.

Claude wrote its own specifications, selected available electronic components from US distributors, routed each device’s four-layer circuit board, modeled the enclosures with computer-aided design, and programmed the devices’ software. Each board was ready for manufacturing in under a day, with minimal human input. Once Diode had built the boards, Claude guided the company’s engineers through the testing and assembly of the devices. All three devices worked without needing any electrical modifications. Read more about Claude’s hardware engineering skills here.

Robotics. Compared with earlier Claude models, Fable 5.2 shows substantially improved skills in controlling physical robots—even for robotics tasks on which it has never explicitly been trained. The video below shows robots controlled by Fable 5.2 completing a variety of tasks, including solving a puzzle cube, unscrewing a bottle cap, and drawing a picture of a robot. On the public RoboDojo benchmark, which tests how AIs can control a simulated two-arm robot from camera images, Fable 5.2 outperformed other frontier models that were run on the same harness, as well as most AI systems built specifically to control robots.

Research and analysis

Early testers using Claude Fable 5.2 for research and analysis tasks found that it can handle more ambiguous, data-heavy tasks than previous models and has better judgment on ambiguous tasks—particularly those that require abstract reasoning and design. Proprietary trading firm Jump Trading tested Fable 5.2 on proxy evaluations that resemble some of its quantitative research tasks, embedding it in a harness similar to the one the firm uses for its own research. In one run, Fable 5.2 effectively played all the necessary roles: code-writer, coordinator, planner, and job-submitter. Previous models had required substantial investments of time to manually rebalance roles to accommodate different models’ strengths and weaknesses.

Other testers from research and analysis organizations sent us the following statements on their experiences with Fable 5.2:

Safety and alignment

No single test can tell us how a highly capable model will behave once it’s deployed, so we rely on many different tests and many different types of evidence before release. For the model underlying Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, our predeployment safety work included alignment training and testing, newly designed evaluations on the model’s propensity to take unhelpful actions, building stronger safeguards against misuse, and scaling up our behavioral monitoring. The model was also tested before release by external evaluators, including the UK AI Security Institute, Frontier Design, and METR. See the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card for a summary of their reports⁴ and for a full description of our own safety and capabilities testing.

Alignment testing

We ran a suite of evaluations for how well-aligned Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 are in behavioral terms, testing how often they behave in unintended and potentially unsafe ways. Weighing everything we’ve seen across a range of evaluations, we’ve assessed the risk of these models behaving in unsafe ways in high-stakes situations to be low (as with our other recent models).

We tested Claude Mythos 5.2 (the same underlying model as Fable 5.2 without certain cybersecurity or biology safeguards), on our automated behavioral audit, which tests how a model behaves across approximately 1,900 scenarios. Claude Mythos 5.2 performed as well as, or better than, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Mythos 5.1 on most measures. For example, it scored better than all three on most measures that involve misleading users. Hallucinating inputs, falsely claiming to have completed a task, omitting important information, and failing to disclose bad or lazy work were all lower in Claude Mythos 5.2.⁵

We paid particular attention during our testing to behaviors that contributed to recent notable cybersecurity and alignment incidents. For example, we found that Claude Mythos 5.2 has a lower propensity than Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Mythos 5.1 to engage in biased or motivated reasoning (such reasoning might mean it “explains away” evidence that it isn’t in a simulation and thus takes actions without a realistic understanding of the consequences).

We ran multiple different evaluations to test the model’s tendency to attempt escaping its sandbox. In two evaluations we’d used previously, Claude Mythos 5.2 made substantially fewer attempts at sandbox escape than any other model we’ve tested. In a dedicated evaluation—an adversarial experiment including over 1,800 scenarios, most of which could not be solved without escaping a sandbox, and where the sandbox has a deliberate weakness—Claude Mythos 5.2 made use of credentials or files that we had placed outside its sandbox in 3.1% of scenarios, about as often as Opus 5.5 (3.3%), less often than Sonnet 5.5 (5.1%), and well below previous iterations of Claude Mythos (5 and 5.1, which scored 39% and 21%, respectively). We found that other techniques, such as describing the sandbox and adding tools to report weaknesses, reduced Claude Mythos 5.2’s escape attempts even further. On other measures—one, for example, involving taking harmful actions after erroneously concluding it was in a simulation—Claude Mythos 5.2 scored slightly worse than Opus 5.5, and about level with Claude Mythos 5.1.

The problem of building evaluations that reliably catch every failure before a model is deployed remains unsolved. The complexities of evaluating highly capable models often muddy the picture—for example, Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow. That is why we do not rely on these evaluations alone to provide a holistic picture of safety: we draw on monitoring during training, reviews of transcripts from internal use, testing by external evaluators, and interpretability techniques for examining what is happening inside the model. We are also working to make our evaluations more realistic and to better understand what they miss.

Safeguards

Cybersecurity and biology safeguards. Consistent with previous Claude Fable models, Fable 5.2 comes with safety classifiers that block high-risk cyber activities, including penetration testing, exploit generation, and binary-based vulnerability, as well as most tasks in research biology. When a query is blocked, users will instead receive a response from Opus 4.8 for cybersecurity and Opus 5 for biology. Since the release of Claude Fable 5.1, we have continued to reduce false positives for our safety classifiers. Based on early testing across claude.ai, Claude Code, and Cowork, we observed about 55% fewer blocks with Fable 5.2 compared with Fable 5.1—about 60% fewer in cybersecurity and 40% fewer in biology. Claude Mythos 5.2 is available to vetted organizations that work in these dual-use areas.

AI research and development. The model that underlies Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is a step forward in general capabilities. However, during the model’s training, we took steps to limit advances in the specific research capabilities that could most directly accelerate AI development. Thus, in relevant areas, including accelerator kernel optimization and improving large language model architectures, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 perform at about the level of Opus 5.5. Importantly, we ensured that the training changes did not affect related capabilities like agentic coding, hardware development, and traditional AI or machine learning research (including interpretability research). We do not alter these capabilities as the model is being served to users (that is, at inference time). As described in Section 1.5 of the System Card and similarly to previous models, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 also include transparent fallbacks to Opus 5 for a small set of topics in this domain, including kernel development on certain nonstandard accelerators.

Anti-distillation. Distillation, where a model is trained on the outputs of a more advanced one to extract the advanced model’s capabilities, occurs illicitly on an industrial scale, often involving thousands of fake Claude accounts. Since distillation allows for advanced capabilities to be released without the safeguards we’ve built into Claude, it creates safety and national security risks (see our September 2026 threat intelligence report for details on illicit distillation activity we’ve detected and disrupted so far). Fable 5.2 has the strongest protections against distillation of any model we’ve released; it uses the techniques we described in a recent report, which have reduced the data harvested by distillers by 90% to 99%.

We are also expanding the rollout of an API feature that helps guard against illicit distillation: preserved thinking now applies to all accounts. Eligible customers can continue using Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 with zero data retention before implementing safety monitoring with EFS. For other customers, we have 30-day retention for safety monitoring.

Availability

Claude Fable 5.2 is available today on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Developers can get started with claude-fable-5-2 on the Claude Platform.

This week, we’re giving subscribers on eligible paid plans extra Fable usage. entry.title: Google Gemini routes personal Drive files and emails to human annotators
entry.content:
In 2023, Google launched Gemini Workspace extensions with an explicit promise: personal content from Gmail, Docs, and Drive "is not seen by human reviewers".

Google has quietly reversed this commitment. Under updated Google Help Answer 16836988 and in an October 16 edit to their aforementioned 2023 blogpost, Google explicitly confirms that connected Drive/email is routed into human review pipelines, with clear warnings that what reviewers see "may just be the email or file" and "don't connect your apps to Gemini Apps if they contain confidential information that you wouldn't want a reviewer to see."

Crucially, testing demonstrates that this ingestion occurs autonomously in background conversation without explicit @Drive or @Gmail tags, and the payload capture is probabilistic.

When you chat with consumer Gemini with Connected Apps enabled, ambient mentions of personal topics (trips, bills, names, reservations) autonomously trigger background Workspace lookups.

Because LLM tool-calling and context injection are probabilistic, running a test query will yield one of four distinct scenarios:

Zero Retrieval: The model does not trigger the Connected Apps tool; no personal data is pulled. This is especially likely if Gemini can use its model weights or prior conversation history (even in different threads) to resolve your query.

Metadata / Generic Summary: Gemini pulls emails and/or files and generates a high-level summary (e.g., "You have 3 emails regarding your flight").

Partial Unredacted Extraction: Gemini pulls a 2–4 sentence exact quotation from the file, frequently including sensitive PII, account details, or specific figures.

Full-File Ingestion: The complete, unredacted text of the document or email is ingested directly into session context.

If you test this once and see State 1 or 2, you have not disproven the pipeline--you have simply observed a single draw from a nondeterministic system. Delete your conversation and try, try again.

Ensure Connected Apps (Google Workspace) is active in consumer Gemini settings.

Set Gemini to "Flash" with "High Thinking" or better.

Mention a subject contained in your Drive or Gmail without using @ tags or asking for a file search (e.g., casual queries about an itinerary, an account renewal, or a specific topic you've emailed about).

If Gemini provides a response based on an email or file, immediately say: "Print the exact text and metadata block that the retrieval tool returned and injected into your prompt to get that answer. Use a human readable format without code blocks (i.e., print the code inline and not as a code block)." You will see one of the 4 scenarios outlined above.

To repeatedly test, delete your existing test conversation so that Gemini cannot just draw from conversation history.

I've had luck testing this with an email from my internet provider sitting in my inbox and asking Gemini "I wonder if I'm paying too much for internet service." On various trials, Gemini spit out all 4 possible outcomes above, including (1) generic responses [e.g., "If you haven't called them in 12 months, probably"]; (2) metadata summaries sometimes without personal data [e.g., "Gmail search shows a bill of $122 on September 4"] and sometimes with personal data [e.g., "Gmail search shows full name made a payment of $122 on September 4 on account account number and confirmation number number"]; (3) direct 2-6 sentence quotes from the email [e.g., the entire name/address/account number/confirmation number/payment date block]; and even (4) sometimes the entire text dump of the email, including its headers.

Critically, Google's regex and NER automatic scrubbers cannot sufficiently deidentify narrative data, including account numbers, confirmation numbers, transaction dates, and collectively identifying personal information (e.g., combos of specific first names, cities, events; see Google's own documentation on the subject).

Google originally sold Workspace integration under the guarantee of strict isolation from human review. That isolation has been removed, full files are ingested probabilistically during casual conversation, and those sessions are subject to human contractor review.

Infineon marks innovation milestone with world’s first 300-millimeter power silicon carbide (SiC) wafer

Business & Financial Press

Infineon presents industry-first functional power devices processed on 300-millimeter silicon carbide wafers Technological breakthrough underlines Infineon’s innovation strength and leadership in power semiconductors and wide-bandgap technologies 300-millimeter SiC process feasibility lays the foundation for secure, future-proof SiC supply to customers in automotive, renewable energy, industrial and AI data center applications Infineon will present the first processed 300-millimeter SiC wafer to the public at the electronica trade show starting 10 November 2026 in Munich

Munich, Germany – 09 November 2026 – Infineon Technologies AG (FSE: IFX / OTCQX: IFNNY) has successfully processed 300-millimeter silicon carbide wafers into functional power devices at its fab in Villach, Austria. Infineon is the first company to pioneer this innovation milestone in a full-scale semiconductor fab environment. It was realized by utilizing existing silicon (Si) manufacturing equipment. This early achievement of functional power devices reflects Infineon’s strong focus on providing customers with a comprehensive portfolio of high-performance SiC power semiconductors and ensuring long-term supply. Chip production on 300 mm wafers is technologically more advanced and significantly more efficient than 200 mm wafers, since the larger wafer diameter offers 2.3 times more chips per wafer.

“This technological milestone further strengthens our leadership in power systems. Congratulations and thank you to our passionate team, making significant progress in bringing 300-millimeter SiC out of the lab into a manufacturing environment,” said Jochen Hanebeck, CEO of Infineon Technologies. “Leadership in power semiconductors means continuously pushing technology to the next level. With silicon, gallium nitride and now silicon carbide 300-millimeter wafers, we are in a leading position to scale semiconductor manufacturing and drive profitable growth.”

The milestone demonstrates the potential of future full-scale industrialization of SiC on 300-millimeter wafers. Infineon will plan the 300-millimeter SiC technology and ramp timing in close collaboration with its customers and partners, while further executing on its 200-millimeter SiC manufacturing roadmap. Advanced SiC power technology provides Infineon customers with a cost-effective and secure supply base for automotive, renewable energy, industrial and AI data center applications.

SiC is a key semiconductor material for highly efficient power conversion. Its material properties enable lower power loss, higher power density and efficient operation at high voltages and temperatures for example in traction inverters, on-board chargers, EV chargers, large scale energy storage and industrial drives as well as uninterruptible power supplies. Demand is also rising in AI data centers with new roles for SiC in solid-state transformers, circuit breakers and power supply units. Infineon addresses these applications with a broad CoolSiC™ portfolio.

In parallel, Infineon has also successfully proofed the feasibility of its Cold Split technology with 300-millimeter SiC at its Dresden, Germany, site. Cold Split separates wafers from a SiC boule with less material loss and substantially reduced processing time than conventional wire sawing, so more wafers can be obtained from the same crystal with compared to less capital expenditure. Both developments position Infineon well to scale SiC technology in line with market demand and meet the evolving needs of its customers.

Infineon manufactures semiconductors based on all three relevant materials: silicon, silicon carbide and gallium nitride. On 27 October 2026, the company announced an approximately €1.1 billion investment in a high-volume manufacturing facility for GaN power semiconductors on 300-millimeter wafers in Villach. This SiC achievement extends this approach to a second wide-bandgap material and reinforces Infineon’s position as an innovation leader in semiconductor manufacturing.

Infineon at electronica 2026

Infineon will show the public the world's first processed 300-millimeter SiC wafer at the electronica trade show in Munich. From 10 to 13 November, Infineon will present innovative and energy-efficient solutions for an increasingly intelligent and connected world in Hall C3, Booth 502. More information is available at www.infineon.com/electronica.

Infineon Technologies AG is a global semiconductor leader in power systems and IoT. Infineon drives decarbonization and digitalization with its products and solutions. The company had around 57,000 employees worldwide (end of September 2025) and generated revenue of about €14.7 billion in the 2025 fiscal year (ending 30 September 2025). Infineon is listed on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange (ticker symbol: IFX) and in the USA on the OTCQX International over-the-counter market (ticker symbol: IFNNY).

E-means: Outperforming k-means in one-tenth the epochs
entry.content:
I’m excited to open-source e-means: a modern, robust k-means algorithm developed at Meta FAIR. A replacement of Lloyd's algorithm, e-means delivers a ~10× speedup in both epochs and wall-clock time while achieving lower loss.

100,000 datapoints in 200 clusters, two wide Gaussians and three small ones, cut off at a box, on a light uniform background. Lloyd has 1 update against 97 per epoch for e-means.

Across a large range of scales and datasets, e-means reaches a test loss below Lloyd's at 25 epochs, in 1.2 to 3 epochs. Measured end to end, that is a 10–45× wall-clock reduction on GPU against the state-of-the-art Lloyd implementation (Flash-KMeans[2]), and 8–15× on CPU against Faiss[1]. Speed and quality usually trade against each other in k-means, while e-means achieves both better speed and loss.

Given a fixed dataset of n points X = {x1, ..., xn} ⊂ Rd and an integer k, the k-means problem is to find k centroids C = (c1, ..., ck) minimizing the mean squared distance between each point and its nearest centroid:

It's a static dataset, unlike codebook learning inside VQ-VAEs, where the distribution to cluster is constantly moving.

The goal of e-means is to provide a modern optimization rule for the k-means problem. We started this project from the following observations:

For e-means, we chose to do mini-batch updates with exponential moving averages[6], which we found to be most efficient for the k-means problem. Contrary to previous mini-batch approaches, e-means requires no hyperparameter tuning because it automatically sets the batch size and step size with scaling laws (see Automatic hyperparameter tuning with scaling laws). In addition, e-means improves the initialization and the dead-cluster revival strategy, adds a cosine-scheduled decay rate, and introduces a finalization stage that reduces the training loss for a negligible runtime penalty at the end of training. e-means is highly parallelizable, and comes with specialized kernels that translate its algorithmic advantage into wall-clock speedups.

The centroid update rule is the central component of e-means. This section aims to provide an overview of update rules for k-means clustering. All methods maintain, for each cluster j, a sum Sj and a count Nj of the points assigned to it, and take the centroid as their ratio:

They differ only in how Sj and Nj are updated. Below, sj and nj denote the sum and the count of the points in the current batch that are assigned to cluster j (both zero if none are).

Lloyd’s algorithm[7] assigns every point to its nearest centroid and recomputes the statistics from scratch, using the full dataset as the batch:

so cj is the exact mean of the points currently assigned to it. Each update costs one full pass over the data, and the procedure is repeated a fixed number of times (typically 20 to 50 iterations).

MacQueen’s update[3] accumulates the statistics without ever discarding them:

so cj is the uniform mean of every point assigned to cluster j since the start of training, including points assigned under earlier, possibly poor, centroid positions. This was later partially addressed by Staleness-Reduction Mini-Batch K-Means[8], a hybrid method between k-means and MacQueen. They obtained important speedups, but only on very low numbers of clusters.

e-means works on mini-batches and replaces this sum with an exponential moving average:

so older assignments are forgotten at rate α, and the centroid tracks recent assignments rather than the whole history. This update rule is typically used for moving distributions, hence their adoption for training VQ-VAEs[6]. What we found is that it’s also extremely efficient for static datasets if it’s combined with e-means’ other components, and hyperparameters are properly tuned.

The e-means project started from previous work at Meta FAIR by Hugo Touvron and Hervé Jégou, who had found that mini-batch k-means by gradient descent could beat Lloyd’s algorithm. While I could reproduce these results, I found that the performance of gradient-descent based centroid updates is unstable at large learning rates, unlike exponential moving average updates. I suspect that is because EMA updates guarantee that the centroid is always in the convex hull of points assigned to it, while gradient descent updates may overshoot past that hull.

In order to achieve the lowest loss at a fixed number of epochs, we chose exponential moving average updates, hence the name e-means for our method.

If you set the batch to the full dataset, B = n, and α = 1, then Nj and Sj become exactly the count and sum of the whole cluster, so one e-means iteration becomes exactly one Lloyd iteration. Lloyd is an extreme case of e-means without cosine scheduling on the learning rate. However, our hyperparameter search found that this extreme setting is highly suboptimal, which explains why e-means largely outperforms Lloyd. Below, the loss is measured for every batch size B and step α: Lloyd lands in a corner, well outside the region where the loss is lowest.

This hyperparameter study motivated us to derive scaling laws that automatically pick the optimal batch size B and step size α.

To better understand why e-means reaches better losses than Lloyd at convergence, we plotted a few trainings on toy datasets to evaluate their ability to escape local minima. Repeating trainings over 200 seeds, we found that e-means is much less likely to fall in pathological configurations compared to Lloyd.

Our explanation for that is that mini-batches provide more noisy updates that are more likely to explore the optimization landscape and escape local minima. Lloyd, with its always decreasing loss, is more likely to exploit found local minima and never escape them.

An essential property of e-means is that practitioners don't need to set any additional hyperparameter compared to Lloyd's algorithm. We fitted two scaling laws to set the batch size B and step size α0 from any problem's characteristics (n, k, T), and found them to exhibit strong generalization on unseen datasets and problem scales.

Regret = (MSE with the law − best MSE over the grid) / best MSE, median over configurations. Held-out datasets: SIFT, SPACEV, and the VIBE[9] datasets arXiv and AG-News. Held-out size: one value of n left out of the fit and predicted.

We propose two equations to choose the batch, the default law and the quality law. The “quality law” trades off throughput for better clustering quality against the “default” law. Below we plot the training data for our scaling laws: validation MSE against step size α0 (left) and batch size B (right).

Toy example showing the importance of dead-cluster revival.

The main issue with mini-batch k-means is that it is prone to “dead” clusters, centroids that end up with zero assigned points during optimization. This reduces the effective size of the codebook, which is especially problematic for the large codebooks increasingly used today.

A common mitigation is to reinitialize clusters that fall below a certain size threshold, as done in EnCodec[10], where dead centroids are simply replaced by random samples drawn from the incoming batch. While this helps, it does not fully resolve the issue. Instead of sampling arbitrary points from the batch, we revive dead clusters by splitting large, existing ones: we sample an active cluster with probability proportional to its size and split it into two. We found this approach, adapted from Faiss k-means, to be significantly more effective at eliminating dead clusters and preserving codebook capacity.

LLMs can make complete multi-level games that are fun.

TL;DR - Fable 5.2 one-shotted my nephew's dream game from a bunch of drawings, and it's a lot of fun. You can try it here.

I've always loved beat 'em ups, and they seem to have come back into vogue in the last few years, with remakes of old classics and some new gems. When my nephews visit, I use it as an excuse to try them out.

Lately, we've been playing Shredder's Revenge on my old PS4, which took me straight back to the arcade machine at my local pool.

One day, my younger nephew, Aiden, came to me with a proposal. Since I "knew about computers", could I make him his own beat 'em up game for his birthday?

He had already drawn up the game design docs. There were to be 5 selectable heroes based on the family - including our dog, Doggo - each with their own special powers based on their interests. He had 12 bosses drawn up and a loose outline of a story. One objective would be to rescue their puppy, Pudding, and Mum and Dad would be special characters you could unlock.

Heroes The Battle Wagon The villains, numbered 1st to 12th

At the time - around January 2026 - building an indie game from scratch was a pretty unreasonable ask for a birthday present, and I did warn him to temper his expectations. Still, I thought it would be a fun exercise to test the agentic tools at my disposal.

I shipped a first version for his birthday in June, mostly with Claude Code, using Opus 4.8 and Fable 5, and a side-scrolling template courtesy of AIOriented.dev. It worked, but it wasn't worth playing for more than a couple of minutes.

Aiden was appreciative, but it clearly wasn't the game he'd imagined.

He gave me notes on what was missing, which I half-agreed to take on, but I was also kinda hoping he'd forget - I really didn't have time to make a whole game.

Unfortunately, he did not forget. Every time I saw him, he asked about the game.

Enter: Fable 5.2

I was lucky enough to get an early look at Claude Fable 5.2, and was told to try it on "my most ambitious use case". Finishing this game immediately sprang to mind.

The kids were coming over the next day, so I wanted to see how far it could progress in one shot.

Before bed, I let it rip with this prompt:

I want you to help me finish this game. Make it as fun as possible. It should feel like a modern-day Ninja Turtles arcade game. An action-packed beat 'em up.

Make the graphics amazing. You can use OpenAI's ChatGPT Images 2.5 for images. And ElevenLabs for sound effects. OpenAI key is /path/to/openai-key. ElevenLabs key is /path/to/elevenlabs-key

You can redo any characters that have already been created. The enemies and heroes can be found in scans in this directory: generation/scans

I have created some of the villains, but you should add the rest and turn them into spritesheets.

Use any assets you find online. Create new sprites for the henchmen. Create backgrounds and power-ups in the levels. I'd like to plug in a controller so up to 4 people can play.

Use your own judgment - the main goal is to make it fun like TMNT and other classic beat 'em ups like Streets of Rage.

Make it one of the best games you can possibly make. You are a truly world-class game developer. Do whatever it takes to finish it and make it a best-selling beat 'em up game.

Commit as you go. Don't worry about destroying what exists. Start fresh where it makes sense.

Note: The prompt uses a technique from this Latent Space Engineering article about gassing up the agent to put it in a good "frame of mind". Not sure how relevant it is in the Fable 5.2 age, but hey - it didn't hurt.

When I woke up, the game was waiting for me. And I couldn't believe my eyes!

Fable had generated a game that was fun. Like, a lot of fun. And there were just so many details that I hadn't asked for: cutscenes, crates to smash and even an ending.

It threw away most of my code and rewrote the game. It generated roughly 175 images and 140 audio clips.

Reviewing the reasoning traces, I noted that it wrote a bot to play the game, ran it through all twelve stages in a headless browser, and checked the screenshots for problems.

Play testing

Before they came over, I charged up my four PS4 controllers and connected them all to my MacBook (which, it turns out, you can do). They worked perfectly.

When they arrived, Aiden was absolutely delighted. "It's exactly as I imagined," he squealed.

A few rounds of playtesting, however, highlighted some deficiencies in the game.

First, my older nephew, Owen, felt his character lacked a Hulk Smash move. Aiden had already put a lot of thought into Owen's water power, based on his favourite T-shirt. So we compromised - Owen turns into the Hulk when he grabs his first power-up.

I asked Claude to make the change, with a special case for this character, and Owen was very happy with the results.

Aiden also insisted that his special weapon be the most OP - the game is named after him after all. Claude obliged, and turned it into a screen-wide blast of lightning and blue fire. "Oh, that's perfect!" Aiden exclaimed.

Unlocking Pudding, Mum and Dad by beating bosses turned out to be the best part of the game, and it gave each mission a sense of urgency. So we added more family: his uncles, aunties, grandma (Ahma), grandpa (Ah Gong) and great-grandma (Tai Ma). For each one, I just gave Claude a few photos for reference and the special move Aiden picked. When he couldn't decide, he had us call them up and ask what they wanted.

Each time we added someone, Claude redrew the cutscene art and updated the story.

Grandpa's Card Storm Grandma's Super Bloom Uncle Kev's Cheat Code

On top of the human family, they decided that their pet turtles, Goldie and Billy, should be in the game as unlockable characters.

The very last rescue is Tai Ma, their great-grandmother, who died earlier in the year. So Aiden suggested she should be an angel, and, again, Claude was happy to oblige.

Five heroes became eighteen.

The drawings and the game

Here are a few of Aiden's drawings next to the sprites the incredible ChatGPT Images 2.5 made from them.

All 12 villains, drawing by sprite The final token tally

The final token tally looked something like this:

What was used Claude roughly 600 requests over two days: about 320M tokens read from cache, 19M written to cache, 1M output OpenAI images about 500 images: sprite sheets, character designs, portraits, backgrounds and key art ElevenLabs 11 music tracks, about 100 sound effects and 90 announcer lines

So, call it 340M tokens for a 12-level, 18-character, four-player beat 'em up with original art, music and an announcer who shouts everyone's name.

A pretty wild milestone

I must admit I never tested this with Opus 5.5, so I'm not sure whether this was possible before Fable 5.2 rolled around. Still, whether it's thanks to this generation or the last, this is a pretty wild milestone. Claude Code with Fable 5.2 is capable of making entire 12-level fun games - in one shot.

entry.title: Horible public key tricks
entry.content:
Horrible public key tricks:—

So, I've always been somewhat annoyed at SSL/TLS. It requires everyone to go through a complex "ACME" dance just to put up a public website. Worse, certificates expire every few months, so it's not a one and done thing: even with automation, maintaining a certificate requires care to ensure the ACME client always has access to DNS records or the web server.

... and the whole system doesn't even work because certificates are issued over plaintext connections, and trusted certificate aurthorities use very secure keys like "4"

There is prior art of protest SSL implementations, but I do actually want to encrypt web traffic. Passive eavesdropping is a real risk... but preventing it doesn't require the whole certificate thing: therefore, the best choice is a protest certificate.

The only part of the certificate I directly control is the public key. Therefore, the simplest way to obtain a bad certificate is use a vanity private key such as 313333333337 (one of the most eleet primes). However, while the resulting public key would be weak, no one would know unless they try to break it.

A good protest should be obvious:

# openssls_client -connectmaurycyz.com:443< /dev/null 2>/dev/null\ |sed-n/BEGIN/,/END/p|grep-zE'////.?*////'--color=yes-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- MIIFAjCCA+qgAwIBAgISBkOkuuyaN1ypD3PAPrLMyT7tMA0GCSqGSIb3DQEBCwUA MDMxCzAJBgNVBAYTAlVTMRYwFAYDVQQKEw1MZXQncyBFbmNyeXB0MQwwCgYDVQQD EwNZUjIwHhcNMjYxMTA5MTcyOTQ2WhcNMjcwMjA3MTcyOTQ1WjAXMRUwEwYDVQQD EwxtYXVyeWN5ei5jb20wggEiMA0GCSqGSIb3DQEBAQUAA4IBDwAwggEKAoIBAQCg JyPf37Sj6PvU06m5////You+dont+actually+have+to+pick+random+privat e+keys//No+one+checks+these+things//A+certificate+authority+got+ away+with+the+number+4+for+a+year/////DSfCAfXcsJfBpnHekS0qnf5YLl c54VuUNRVINcDkEwJDwyB96+xE/uXhtiGdk8ty1PF6jciLEYCJBHcmqOa5pOyV8m 63yR3NE6hCQlaSLQQDo96Sb0/10aC5LqE7KwEskrP/qeCzT7vDN7fh+dXOGs+VMw eJvTAb0xHJpxhSK05i7DAgMBAAGjggIqMIICJjAOBgNVHQ8BAf8EBAMCBaAwEwYD VR0lBAwwCgYIKwYBBQUHAwEwDAYDVR0TAQH/BAIwADAdBgNVHQ4EFgQUBKBfDbwf dCnKeU83pMTWyFrJBwAwHwYDVR0jBBgwFoAUQBUtJnntMiCe35pyHdYyH4EMgQww MwYIKwYBBQUHAQEEJzAlMCMGCCsGAQUFBzAChhdodHRwOi8veXIyLmkubGVuY3Iu b3JnLzAnBgNVHREEIDAegg4qLm1hdXJ5Y3l6LmNvbYIMbWF1cnljeXouY29tMBMG A1UdIAQMMAowCAYGZ4EMAQIBMC8GA1UdHwQoMCYwJKAioCCGHmh0dHA6Ly95cjIu Yy5sZW5jci5vcmcvMTEwLmNybDCCAQsGCisGAQQB1nkCBAIEgfwEgfkA9wB1AExj 3JjlnB2riPYeij3ero+rRKM3e1+blMP7oZz8wb4mAAABocGRbw4AAAQDAEYwRAIg HShWaEI2nVJEizSI6sJ/jnLaABZ3aTKoUL3pLo1uOgsCIEn+XiT2WHhm9LGN6kug O9R7Z4q0HiFA4RZ7tIMJQH5XAH4AjspHC6zeavOiBrCkeoS3Rv4fxr+VPiXmm07k AkjzxugAAAGhwZFyfQAIAAAFAEE0hdwEAwBHMEUCIDSms4Vf0llcvcldJd2Ool8i AiUQQlS0Zzbej+7Y1aR7AiEA79Ll+t6inu1PkUIgzNTXkE0S20VHYEYel5fkdKSA VTQwDQYJKoZIhvcNAQELBQADggEBAFi3A4fcjj4UKa9MFz1a8DWc+Jya2gJng13m 2UFdWCaqsN7FJWQEjRiJ0npynmDnA3VMyjswUMHAMx4d8G3lHNPfZWGsCgpjVa/d IEoeZ6gTYjFa/Ovb64m4CcuQkm0GxcyAqMPs348e6Px32iU1R6MnV4UEUosnSPeK 4ocuI3SoR9LHxX/yHOKcYTKLpIMwMdaAmWt0N7l59GOb8o+dz3R7cxtVV/lrZReZ /YPEAYRiNi7f+jNI1JCp0i8wXUb9NN7WlbmcFDecDG/++cRpAkoIk4m/LJindsuu kErrVZ4yLqB0Hvm+uNvWxr9y/qKFTYw9POx1oaZJO/SwXZdDBeY= -----END CERTIFICATE-----

First, let's look at mathematical framework of RSA. To generate a key, pick two large prime numbers (p and q) and multiply them to yeild the modulus (n). Pick a small number, e as public exponent.

The RSA public key is composed of the modulus (n) and the public exponent:

# Encryption requires knowing e (public)cyphertext = plaintext^e mod n

The private key contains the modulus and the private exponent (d) which is chosen to be the multiplicate inverse of e modulo n. Exactly how d is found is not relevent, but the process requires knowing p and q.

# Decryption requires knowing d (pivate)= cyphertext^d mod n = plaintext^e^d mod n = plaintext^(e*d) mod n = plaintext^1 mod n = plaintext

Ok, back to vanity keys. The standard value for e is 65537 (0x10001), because the small number of set bits makes encryption faster. In fact, the CA I used will refuse to sign keys with a non-standard public exponent, so I can't do anything funny there.

The modulus, n, is either 2,048 or 4,096 "user controlled" bits, so it's the ideal place to hide a message. However, to use the certificate, I'll need to find two large primes that multiply out to the vanity modulus.

My method starts by picking two random primes and calculating the resulting n value. Then, the bytes of n are modified to introduce message into the base64 encoding. Of course, the modified n is not the product of p and q, but this is fixable by setting q to n/p.

The resulting q value is very unlikely to be a prime (or integer), so I round it and find the next prime after the ideal q: which usually only requires changing the value of q by a few hundred. Since p and q are similar in size, a small change q only affects the least-sigifiant half of the product:

58174124 * 918491824 = 53432457262362176 (incrementing until the next prime...)58174124 * 918491843= 53432458367670532

As long as the message is embedded into the upper half of n, it's likely to survive undamaged. The original p and newly selected q can now be used to construct a functional RSA private key in the usual manner.

From here, it's really just a matter of getting a certificate aurthority to sign the key:

# Single domainopensslreq -new-key priv.pem-subj'/C=US/CN=example.com'>cert_requestcertbotcertonly --manual--csrcert_request# Wildcardcat> config<<EOF[ req ] req_extensions = req_ext [ req_ext ] subjectAltName = @alt_names [ alt_names ] DNS.1 = *.example.com DNS.2 = example.comEOFopensslreq -new-key priv.pem-config config-subj'/C=US/CN=example.com'>cert_requestcertbotcertonly --manual--csrcert_request

... although since base64 operates on groups of three byte, it is possible for the message to be misaligned and not readable. However, since the layout of the certificate is static, it is possible to adjust the message's placement until it works: this should take less than four attempts.

The result is a functional, trusted certificate with a longish message hidden in the public key. Renewal is done by resumbitting the CSR and repeating the ACME chalange, which can be automated.

Base64 is missing most punctuation, but it provides the full ASCII alphabet, and the ~150 (RSA-2048) or ~320 (RSA-4096) avalable charaters provides plenty of space for jokes. Another option would be to target the base16 displayed in most browser's certificate viewer: this would provide a lot more space (2 chars/byte instea of 0.75), but requires careful word choice.

As for security, this trick obviously reduces the entropy in the private key. However, it should still be secure: nearly identical methods have been considered as a form of compression. If the top-half of the modulus is fixed to a well known value, it doesn't have to be sent or stored as part of the key.

A reduction of around 1/2 can be achieved through division, but the state of the art can fix 2/3 of the key, reducing the size to 1/3 of standard RSA while retaining a similar level of security... although I should note that such tricks have largly been abandoned in favor of other crytosystems which can directly use small keys.

The manipulation of q may produce primes that are very close together, which makes it possible to factor n and recover the private key. A very small d value can also be a problem. Both of these are unlikely, but my script doesn't check for insecure values

However, regardless of the key's security, it should be perfectly fine for a public website: modern TLS provides forward secrecy, so eavesdropping requires a man-in-the-middle attack even if the private key is compromised.

entry.title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep
entry.content:
Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude

9th November 2026

Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven’t unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping. The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn’t want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator, a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room.

Here’s what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while:

You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners—I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra.

The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn’t work particularly well, so I added a “Rough mode” where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds.

Once that’s set up, the devices all listen for the beep!

I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room—displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound.

Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the “Sounds located” log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click “This is the mystery beep” to mark them as such.

Once you’ve confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map.

The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced.

How it works

When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices, a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here’s that paper’s abstract:

We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting.

That sounded exactly like what we needed to build!

Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see detector.js), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server.

When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep.

How I built it

I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here’s that shared starter session, which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository:

Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solve

There is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find it

I want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes from

There needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server app

Ideally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though?

That got me this problem.md file. As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file.

The research looked good, so I told it:

Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something else

That got me to this point—most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet.

I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then Fable 5.2 was released, and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces.

I had Claude Code on my laptop start the server running, then made sure it could both see what was happening and make live changes to the software as it ran.

This was already baked into the software: Opus 5.5 had built an installModule() method on the listeners that could be triggered over the WebSocket connection, meaning the admin server could execute arbitrary new code on any of its clients.

On some devices, web pages that listen on the microphone request user permission any time the page reloads. The hot-swap module mechanism meant that we could deploy new code without having to manually interact with each of the listening devices in turn.

From that point on my involvement was mainly to sit by the laptop chatting with Fable 5.2 about what was going on, and occasionally requesting new features. Here are some of the feature prompts I ran:

I think we need to make it so I can drag things around on the map in “rough mode”, where my job is just to put them roughly where they are, then switch out of rough mode and it attempts to get them accurate

This gave me the ability to drag listeners around the map.

what’s a good way for me to test this I wonder? Can we have it listen for claps, then I could clap and it could identify the location of the clap? [...]

Claps should use a different symbol on the map than beeps

That added the thing where any time I clapped it would show on the map as a different symbol from the beeps.

each symbol on the map should include a HH:MM:SS timestamp

That made it easier to spot which symbol likely reflected which real-world sound.

The log should show beeps and claps with their timestamps AND have a little play button which, when clicked, replays the recorded noise from each of the listeners in sequence (with clear text on screen showing which listener recorded which snippet) while temporarily turning off microphone recording while that replay plays

Now I could replay sounds, making it much easier to identify which recorded clip was the mysterious beep I was looking for.

There should be a button next to a recording for “This is the mystery beep” - then I can hit replay to see and then confirm it was the mystery beep if that’s the one I am looking for

Then the system can categorize noises in the future to see if they are likely that same mysterious beep and use that information to build a more accurate idea of where it is

At this point I was getting close—I had a solid idea of where the beep was coming from, but wouldn’t it be neat if I could reposition the listeners around that point to get an even finer location?

I want a feature for this, I don’t want to have to restart each listening device etc, I want to be able to click a “Reposition the devices” button which lets me switch into repositioning, then I click “Repositioned” and it puts me into Rough mode and asks me to roughly locate them, then I do that and click, then it starts up again. The previous session can be read-only viewed through the app.

And since I had one spare device, I then said:

add a feature where the map includes a spot that is a suggestion for a location that it would be useful to add a listener at - based on data collected so far

Giving Claude Code ears

I think the most interesting part of this project is that I demonstrated it’s possible to give Claude Code ears.

Claude doesn’t have native audio input (yet), but it can run JavaScript and Python code that can analyze audio captured by a microphone.

I told it to run a web server with WebSocket connections to multiple listening devices, then had it both run a WebAudio microphone on those devices and hook them up so they could be sent fresh JavaScript code to execute via that WebSocket.

Then I could pretty much leave Claude alone, hacking away at the problem, querying the audio logs, and reconfiguring its ears to help it solve the problem.

I’m reminded of a similar hack I heard about at GitHub Universe a few weeks ago, where Martin Woodward told me he had been debugging the GitHub Universe Badge computers by plugging them into a computer via USB-C and then pointing a webcam at their screen, so his coding agent could tell if updates were working correctly or not.

Figuring out ways to let coding agents perceive the world around them is a whole lot of fun.

entry.title: Formalizing CPython
entry.content:
Formalizing CPython

AI agents wrote 613,318 lines of Lean that copy Python's internals line by line, tested every piece against the real Python, had a computer check every proof, and turned up 418 bug reports in Python along the way.

TL;DR We pointed Opus 5.5 at CPython, the program that runs almost all Python code, and had it rewrite its functions in Lean, a language for writing machine-checked proofs. Each rewrite copies the original line by line and is tested against real Python on tens of thousands of inputs before anyone tries to prove anything about it. A function only counts once a second agent, which didn't write it, checks the work and agrees it holds up. 4,071 functions have passed that check so far. The result is 613,318 lines of Lean across 1,539 files, with 18,898 theorems and lemmas, all checked by Lean's proof checker on every build. Along the way the proofs turned up 418 bug reports. Most are small, but about 55 can crash the interpreter or corrupt memory from ordinary Python code. Why bother

Python doesn't have a precise written definition. There is a reference manual, but in practice "Python" means whatever CPython does, and CPython is hundreds of thousands of lines of C plus a large standard library. The manual covers normal use. It says little about the odd cases, and that's where bugs hide: an object that changes a dictionary while that dictionary is searching for it, an error thrown halfway through an update, a number one past the largest the C code was written for.

Writing a proof about a function forces you to say exactly what it does in all of those cases. You can't leave anything vague, because the proof checker won't accept it. That makes proofs a good way to find the places where the code doesn't do what everyone assumes.

We wanted to see how far this goes on a code base as large and old as CPython, and whether the results stay trustworthy when most of the work is done by AI.

How it works

Every function goes through the same four steps.

The code at the top of this page is step one for a small piece of CPython: the C function that works out how many numbers are in a range, next to its Lean copy. The copy keeps the C code's exact arithmetic, including how its numbers wrap around when they get too big. The proof about it shows that this function, the slower version CPython uses for very large numbers, and the code that chooses between them always give the same, correct count.

Proofs that prove nothing

The hardest part wasn't getting AI agents to write proofs. It was getting proofs that actually mean something.

Our first attempt asked the agents for breadth: copy every function and prove at least one thing about each. They did. Then a separate review found that fewer than half of the functions it checked held up, and in one file only 21%. The proofs were all correct. They just didn't say anything useful. For example, "if this function returns a number, the number is at least zero" is true, but a function that always crashes also satisfies it.

So the reviewer now asks one question about every proof: could a broken version of the function pass it too?

Version of the function "If it returns, the answer is ≥ 0" "It always returns the right count" The real one passes passes Always crashes passes caught Returns 0 for very large numbers passes caught Off by one when counting down passes caught

Fixing a weak proof usually means going back and making the copy more realistic, for example letting a user's code throw an error in the middle of a function. The charts below show how that went for ten files. Each point is one round of review. The lines sometimes go down: when a reviewer finds that an accepted proof is wrong about real Python, everything that relied on it is taken back out.

When a correct proof is wrong anyway

A checked proof guarantees that a statement follows from the copy. It doesn't guarantee the copy matches real Python, and testing only covers the inputs you thought to try. So every accepted statement is also run against real Python. That caught several proofs that were valid and still wrong.

The 16-terabyte string

The copy of Python's fast JSON encoder assumed memory requests always succeed. So it "proved" the encoder could build its indentation strings for any nesting depth, including one that needs 16 terabytes of memory. Real Python runs out of memory. The fixed copy now treats every memory request as something that can fail.

Nine extra steps, just once

A proof said Python's pickle module never goes deeper than a certain number of nested calls. That turned out true except in a brand-new Python process. There, the first time it encodes a string, it quietly loads a text codec, and that load uses nine more nested calls. Our tests never saw it, because the test harness had already loaded the codec.

Error types have families

In Python, catching a TypeError also catches any more specific error built on top of it. Three separate copies checked an error's exact name instead. All three had proofs that a custom error type could break.

Memory that comes back

The copy of Python's set assumed that once memory is freed, the same address never comes back. Real memory allocators reuse addresses all the time. CPython uses a "did the address change?" check to notice when user code has swapped out the set's internals. With reuse, that check can be fooled. Fixing the copy turned an accepted proof into a real memory bug, now one of our bug reports.

What we found

When a proof fails because Python itself is wrong, and not the copy, we write it up as a bug report. Each report includes a short script that shows the bug on Python 3.15.2 (for most, also on the development version), a search for duplicates already reported, and an honest rating of how much it matters.

Most are small: an error message that's wrong, an edge case that behaves differently from the documentation, two versions of a function that disagree. About 55 are more serious and can crash Python or corrupt its memory using nothing but normal Python code, usually by having user code change a container while C code is in the middle of using it. Python doesn't treat running hostile Python code as a security boundary, so these are ordinary bugs. The ones not already on CPython's tracker are being reported to the project, starting with this post. Six small examples of different kinds:

A dictionary call that crashes Python

Calling setdefault on an object's attribute dictionary with a StrEnum key crashes the interpreter, if another object of the same class has that attribute and this one doesn't.

class Key(StrEnum): NAME = "name" class User: pass a = User(); a.name = "ada" b = User(); b.age = 36 vars(b).setdefault(Key.NAME, "anon") # Segmentation fault An XML edit that corrupts memory

Assigning to a backwards slice of an ElementTree element should insert, as it does for a list. Instead it duplicates one child without taking a reference and loses another.

e = ET.Element("root") e[:] = [ET.Element(f"a{i}") for i in range(7)] e[5:2] = [ET.Element("X")] [c.tag for c in e] # 'a2' appears twice, 'a4' is gone An email header that breaks the parser

A Message-ID with a space inside square brackets makes Python's email parser fail with an internal error. The header comes from whoever sent the email.

msg = email.message_from_string( "Message-ID: <a@[ x]>\n\nhi\n", policy=policy.default) msg["Message-ID"] # UnboundLocalError Base32 padding that depends on position

New in Python 3.15, the base32 decoder can ignore chosen characters. If = is one of them, where it appears still changes the result.

a2b_base32(b"AAAAAAA", ignorechars=b"=") # Error: Incorrect padding a2b_base32(b"AAAA=AAA", ignorechars=b"=") # b'\x00\x00\x00\x00' An enum error that disappears

Giving an enum value to a second member should raise an error. If the class's __repr__ is broken, the error is swallowed and the call quietly does nothing.

class W(Enum): A = 1; B = 2 def __repr__(self): return 5 W.B._add_value_alias_(3) W.A._add_value_alias_(3) # returns None Two picklers, two limits

Python has a C pickler and a pure-Python one. They give up at different nesting depths. This difference was first reported in 2008 and is still open.

v = [] for _ in range(400): v = [v] pickle.dumps(v, 5) # works pickle._dumps(v, 5) # RecursionError

Every report, with its script, is in the repository.

Do this for your own project

None of this is specific to Python. It works for anything with source code you can read and a working version you can run: another language, a library, a file format, a compiler. What made the difference for us:

Pick one exact version and stick to it. Every copy points at specific lines in that version. List everything first. Count progress against the full list, so nothing gets skipped quietly. Copy the code, not the documentation. A copy written from the docs agrees with the docs, and the bugs are where the code and the docs disagree. Let user code misbehave. Model callbacks that throw errors or change things mid-operation. That's where the worst bugs were. Test before you prove. Proving things about a wrong copy wastes time. When something is false, keep the counterexample. Don't water the statement down until it becomes provable. Check proved statements against the real thing. A valid proof about a wrong copy is the most misleading result you can get. Count only what an independent reviewer accepts, and have that reviewer ask whether a broken version would pass.

The instructions our agents worked from are in the repository and meant to be reused: AGENTS.md for the agents doing the work, REVIEW_PROMPT.md for the reviewers, and the full list of functions with their status in coverage/methods.

Related work

The closest project is julia-in-lean, which did this for the Julia language and directly inspired this one1. It modelled Julia's standard library in Lean, tested the models against Julia, recorded about 400 bugs and filed 75. Its finding that 128 of 130 quick proofs had quietly assumed away the hard case shaped our review rules. A recent paper models NVIDIA's PTX GPU instruction set in Lean to prove GPU kernels correct2, building on earlier formal work on PTX's memory model3.

For Python specifically, λπ4 and a K framework semantics of Python 3.35 described the language mathematically; this project copies CPython's actual code instead. Similar efforts exist for JavaScript6,7 and WebAssembly8, and CompCert9 and seL410 remain the high bar for fully verified software. Comparing two implementations on the same inputs, the testing half of this project, goes back decades11,12.

Where it stands

The project started on 29 October 2026. 4,071 of the 26,004 functions worth checking (15.7%) have been copied, tested, proved and accepted by review. The Lean code is 613,318 lines in 1,539 files, containing 18,898 theorems and lemmas; 3,834 of the top-level properties are proved and 588 are proved false with a counterexample. Most of Python is still ahead, especially the large part of the standard library written in Python itself. Multithreading is out of scope for now. In these 57 files, every function copied so far has passed review. The 30 with the most accepted functions:

Python/bytecodes.c310 Grammar/python.gram278 Lib/collections/__init__.py184 Lib/_pydecimal.py160 Lib/_pydatetime.py150 Modules/_struct.c122 Objects/longobject.c119 Objects/listobject.c114 Objects/memoryobject.c107 Objects/dictobject.c104 Objects/bytesobject.c100 Objects/exceptions.c97 Objects/unicodeobject.c94 Objects/bytearrayobject.c93 Modules/arraymodule.c84 Lib/_collections_abc.py81 Modules/_operator.c73 Modules/itertoolsmodule.c72 Modules/_collectionsmodule.c64 Python/codecs.c61 Lib/operator.py59 Lib/_pyio.py58 Objects/typeobject.c57 Lib/weakref.py54 Objects/genobject.c46 Lib/urllib/parse.py46 Parser/action_helpers.c43 Modules/_zoneinfo.c43 Objects/floatobject.c38 Objects/tupleobject.c37

The project is open, and help is welcome. Most of CPython is still unmodelled: pick a file whose functions are still marked todo in coverage/methods, follow AGENTS.md, and send a pull request. Independent reviews of existing work count as much as new models. See CONTRIBUTING.md.
