entry.title: CoreWeave bond yield tops 16% as AI credit stress rises
entry.content:
Debt markets are sending a message to AI data center builders: we're hiking the interest rate on your credit card and may put some new curbs on your credit limit.

That analogy comes courtesy of Jefferies global head of equity strategy, Christopher Wood, who put it in a note on Friday: "The most plausible way the AI capex arms race will end is that the credit card will be taken away."

That isn't happening yet, but credit markets have been spooked by the new political landscape — seeing more hurdles to data centers under Democratic governors in key states, along with a Democratic-controlled Congress.

The poster child for debt stress is neocloud Coreweave. The yield on its 2032 bond with a 9.625% coupon has climbed above 16%. Coreweave's five-year credit default swaps spiked above 1,289 basis points on Thursday, widening above their October peak, according to Deutsche Bank. The CDS eased 8% Friday to around 1,155.

"We've had plenty of warnings from the credit space," said Jim Reid, Deutsche Bank's global head of macro and thematic research, in a note on Friday. Debt and equities are now moving more in sync, he added, "so we'll have to see if credit goes any further."

Investors are demanding more compensation to insure against default among even companies with the strongest balance sheets and credit ratings, including Nvidia, Broadcom, and Amazon.com.

CDS on Nvidia debt is up 76% in the last month. Broadcom's CDS is up 49%, while Amazon's has gained 44%. Their CDS remain low on an absolute basis; Nvidia's spread stood at roughly 139 basis points, compared with about 298 bps for Oracle and roughly 1,100 for CoreWeave. A large increase from a low starting point does not imply the same credit risk.

Still, rising CDS are a sign that markets want more protection against default among even the largest and healthiest debt issuers. And rising CDS imply higher financing costs down the line.

The market is now grappling with the prospect that at least some data center spending will be delayed or scrapped under incoming Democratic governors in Ohio, Texas, and Georgia, the three states with much of the planned capacity.

Moratoriums could impact 45% of planned capacity in the U.S. with a large amount of that in Texas, according to Goldman Sachs. Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she's not opposed to data centers but wants a moratorium until the state legislature passes protections for communities.

None of these means AI debt financing is collapsing. Goldman tallies five AI bond deals totaling $67 billion since October 29, pushing total hyperscaler debt issuance this year to $296 billion. Goldman forecasts $440 billion of hyperscaler debt issuance next year, plus an additional $300 billion of project-level issuance across investment-grade and high-yield.

The Trump administration is vowing to support data centers. National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett told CNBC on Friday that he expects data center growth to continue as forecast, despite Democrats' big election wins.

What comes next

The big question now is how quickly AI spending will generate enough cash for hyperscalers to keep investors comfortable with future capex plans. For the neoclouds, any sign of consolidation or retrenchment in capex could result in fewer or shorter contracts for data center compute or delays in prepayments.

Goldman analysts said hyperscalers collectively reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter as capital spending exceeded operating cash flow.

"Delayed monetization and growth in purchase commitments—which we view as additional and sizable uses of cash, separate from Capex—are the key risks to more debt issuance, subject to market conditions," according to the bank.

Peak AI debt issuance may now be closer at hand. Bank of America analysts estimates that AI-related credit issuance will rise 31% from 2026 to 2027, hitting $685 billion, including public and private debt. They then see it falling 23% to $531 billion in 2028.

As for the risk? "Downside to these forecasts exists from a potential slowdown in AI infrastructure projects on the back of the Blue Wave, which will reduce capex needs and thus debt market funding," BofA said in a note.

-CNBC's Nick Wells and Michael Bloom contributed reporting

entry.title: Ultorg: The User Interface for Relational Databases
entry.content:
The missing user interface for

Ultorg is an efficient, spreadsheet-like UI for relational databases. Query and edit data across tables and relationships, without SQL or custom CRUD apps. Watch the conference talk.

MacOS | Windows | Linux14-day free trial

Matías Fernández@matias__eduardo

@ultorg is the most mind blowing database tool I have ever seen. The way it can visualize multiple joins feels canonical in the sense that now, when I run complicated SQL queries, *that’s* the format I use to imagine the results. vimeo.com/695905306

 Gene Kim@RealGeneKim

Jaw dropping talk on a way to view SQL databases without writing a custom app. Imagine Microsoft Access crossed with Microsoft Excel and a big dose of incredible sorcery So exciting!! Can’t wait to learn more about @ultorg

Justin Duke@jmduke

This presentation by @eirikbakke on a generic UI abstraction to navigate a relational database is the most exciting bit of interaction design I've seen in a long, long time. vimeo.com/372006027

Petri Aukia@aukia

The future never came: I expected dynamic multi-dimensional spreadsheet to sooner or later become the norm ever since I saw Lotus Improv. With @ultorg you get to wonder – perhaps the multidimensional UI is to a set of database tables, not to a spreadsheet.

“Harmonic is building mathematical superintelligence. Deep, detailed analysis of our system's outputs is crucial for rapid advancement of our research agenda. Ultorg provides, by far, the best tool for visualizing and investigating our data. It is an invaluable tool for our research.”

Tables of Data

Whether in finance, engineering, operations, or the life sciences, you are likely working with tables of data in spreadsheets, CSV files, or an external database. Spreadsheets are excellent tools for managing a single table of data. They are a poor fit for database tasks, however, where data must be combined and queried in many different ways.

Ultorg is a general-purpose, graphical user interface for relational databases. That means any data that's organized into tables with rows and named columns. Behind the scenes, Ultorg generates SQL queries that execute either remotely or on your local computer.

Connect to:

PostgreSQL Microsoft SQL Server MySQL/MariaDB DuckDB and Parquet Google BigQuery Microsoft Access Files (.mdb/.accdb) Microsoft Excel Files (.xls/.xlsx) Google Sheets CSV/TSV Files Other JDBC-based data sources In beta: Oracle, Snowflake, SQLite, Athena, Exasol Visual Joins

A join is a fundamental database operation that combines data from two different tables, based on a common identifier such as “Room Number” or “Customer ID”. Joins are frequently needed when working with multi-table datasets.

In Ultorg, you can quickly join data from multiple tables or data sources, and interact with the result through a single, spreadsheet-like data manipulation surface.

For SQL-based data sources, Ultorg will recognize existing foreign key relationships, and suggest relevant joins. Or you can join on arbitrary fields, e.g., to combine data from a spreadsheet and a CSV file.

One-to-Many Relationships

A join between two tables will often involve a one-to-many relationship, where each row in the first table can match multiple rows in the second table.

Ultorg will visualize any combination of one-to-many relationships, in a compact but readable way, using a specially developed system of visual data layouts. Sorting, filters, and formulas can be applied at any level, and joins can be chained or included side-by-side without losing or duplicating rows.

Among visual database tools, Ultorg is unique in its ability to handle one-to-many relationships in a general way.

One-to-many relationships also occur inside database queries, when grouping on fields to calculate sums or averages, or when nesting one query within another. Ultorg will visualize each stage of such data flows.

For example, you can see the individual values that contribute to a group-wise sum. This lets you audit the query visually. You can tweak filters and calculations in the input, while gaining confidence in the aggregated totals.

SQL Without SQL

At first glance, Ultorg's direct manipulation interface resembles a spreadsheet. The tabular layout you see on the screen, however, represents a real database query, which can be refreshed and modified without risking changes to the underlying raw data.

A visual query lets you see exactly the data you need for a particular business task, without descending into a code editor, form designer, or flow chart. Even for database experts, Ultorg will serve as a rapid alternative to hand-typed SQL.

Most SELECT queries that can be written in the core SQL language have a visual equivalent in Ultorg. For example, you can express arbitrary combinations of joins, filters, calculations, and subqueries.

Dynamic Autolayout

In business or engineering data, or in the social sciences, you may be dealing with hundreds of fields of various data types—text, numbers, and dates—spread across dozens of tables, each with thousands (or millions) of rows.

To retain sanity, it is essential not to have to spend time tweaking formatting settings for each individual field, or for every new database query.

Ultorg eliminates such hard, manual labor, by analyzing your data on the fly and deriving carefully tuned defaults. For example, label placements, table column widths, text field dimensions, decimal precision, and pagination are all handled automatically. You can see all your data with fewer keystrokes.

Ultorg's typographical engine can visualize records and one-to-many relationships using a combination of general-purpose strategies, such as nested tables, forms, and crosstabs.

Ultorg's visual data layouts are analogous to the hand-designed user interface screens you might see in traditional, tailored database applications. But in Ultorg, they are available immediately, for any data, without custom programming.

Create, Read, Update, Delete

From Ultorg, you can also edit data, stored in a relational database, in a Microsoft Excel workbook, or in Google Sheets.

You can edit values in individual cells, pick values from a dropdown, insert rows, or fill down, like in a spreadsheet.

You can review changes before committing to the database. Multiple users can edit at the same time.

For internal business operations, Ultorg can serve as an alternative to custom CRUD interfaces, or as a way to supercharge your spreadsheet-based recordkeeping.

Connect to Your Data, Right Now

Start Ultorg and connect immediately to your data source. No “cloud” required; all data stays private on your computer or corporate network.

entry.title: Your TV can see through walls
entry.content:
Your TV can see through walls:—

This is a spectogram of the signal from a local TV station:

Walking between the receiver and TV station causes a slight disturbance to the signal, but it's nothing to write home about:

For this capture, I moved the antenna a few centimeters:

This is selective fading: The direct signal is being canceled out by a strong reflection. Because the phase of the reflection depends on frequency, this effect is not uniform over the whole signal. Apart from being annoying if you're trying to watch TV, this state is extremely sensitive to any nearby movement.

Here's what happened to the signal when I got up from my chair:

... and here's me walking around in a neighboring room:

The gaps between the stripes happen when my reflection perfectly cancels out the residual signal, which happens each time the path length changes by one wavelength. Let's use this to figure out how fast I was walking:

The gap between each stripe is around 70 pixels, and the waterfall has an update rate of 150 Hz...

70 pixels * 1 second/150 pixels = 0.47 seconds = 2.1 Hz speed of light / 490 MHz * 2.1 Hz = 1.3 m/s = 4.6 km/h

I was walking perpendicular to the direct signal path, so the speed can be used as is, without any adjustments for geometry.

So, a simple radio reciever is able to detect motion and provide an estimated speed — and it's not just TV that works for this: any wideband radio signal like WiFi or LTE can be used in much the same way. Those make worse demonstrations because they have a messy waterfall, but it's possible extract the same data with a bit of work.

Happy paranoia!

entry.title: Amazon saves millions by replacing Sonnet 4.6 with Strands Decider
entry.content:
For a while, Amazon and AWS teams relied on Claude Sonnet 4.6 to label tickets in an internal system without breaking the bank.

Sonnet 4.6 fit the goldilocks choice of balancing intelligence with cost. Considering it dealt with one of the world’s largest internal ticketing systems, the nine month old model did well. However, two Amazon engineers recently swapped out Sonnet 4.6 for Strands Decider, a decision model we launched a month ago, that performed just as well at 98% less cost. This change will save millions of dollars of token costs in a year.

Carr and Mehul, who work on the internal ticketing system, walk through how this happened below.

Replacing an LLM’s job with a decision model

We had Sonnet 4.6 labeling tickets at enormous scale. The tickets could be customer escalations, capacity requests, automated alarms, security findings, or anything else across the company that needed to fit within 20 category types. The agent ran with a long system prompt on every ticket, generating JSON and reasoning against a fixed set of labels.

A decision model can’t generate text. It’s first given some state and a question with a set of options, then the decision model returns a probability for each option plus a confidence score. We saw this method fit perfectly with ticket labeling: the state is the ticket, the options are the label catalog.

We started with the original Strands Decider 2B. On a test set of tickets, the E4B Gemma 4 build got clearly better results, so we switched to it. Afterwards, we tuned how confident the model needed to be before applying a label. The results showed E4B beating production Sonnet on a separate set of our tickets.

We ran E4B on SageMaker ml.g5.xlarge instances (one A10G, 24 GB each). The model used about 19 GiB, and one request took about 640 ms on one instance. The endpoint autoscales with traffic, but its network was isolated, preventing outbound access to the container. SageMaker copies the model weights in from S3 before start-up.

Customers can do this too! Apart from our ticketing APIs, everything in the path is a standard AWS service. Ticket events land in an SQS queue that then triggers a Lambda function. It reads the ticket data and calls the model, a SageMaker AI Endpoint with Strands Decider. AppConfig holds the switch (described below), and CloudWatch carries the logs, metrics and alarms. The stack is defined in CDK with deployment stages for Beta, Gamma, and Prod.

Running Sonnet 4.6 and Strands Decider on the same tickets

We didn’t want to flip a switch and hope. The labeling Lambda reads a three-way setting from AWS AppConfig on every message:

BEDROCK: Sonnet labels every ticket, but Strands Decider isn’t called. DUAL: Both the Sonnet and Strands Decider models are called in parallel. The results from the Sonnet model are applied to the ticket and compared with Strands Decider results. DECIDER: Strands Decider labels every ticket and Bedrock isn’t called. What we measured Claude Sonnet 4.6 Strands Decider E4B % Improvement Average time per call 4,215 ms 897 ms 78% Input tokens per ticket 6,554 2,009 Output tokens per ticket 170 1 Total tokens, per ticket 6,724 2,010 70%

The token drop had two sources. Strands Decider produced one output, the choice, instead of a JSON answer. Its prompt was also much shorter than Sonnet 4.6’s. Production’s label descriptions alone are longer than Strands Decider’s 4,096-token window, so we rewrote each of the 20 labels as a one- or two-sentence criterion and sent them as the options of a single choice question, plus a “none” option. The ticket data is the same as what Sonnet gets, except that on long tickets Strands Decider drops the oldest comments to fit.

Below is a graph of our Lambda durations on the day we turned off the Sonnet usage, showing the average Lambda execution duration dropping 74%.

What it costs

At published us-east-1 on-demand prices:

Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Bedrock, global endpoint) Strands Decider E4B (SageMaker, ml.g5.xlarge) Price $3.00 per 1M input, $15.00 per 1M output tokens $1.408 per instance-hour Per ticket $0.0222 about $0.0005 Per million tickets about $22,200 about $500

Sonnet’s cost per ticket comes straight from the token counts above. Strands Decider’s depends on how busy each instance is. At about 640 ms per request, one instance can handle about 5,600 tickets an hour, which would be $250 per million tickets at full use. We keep headroom for bursts, and in practice it comes to about $500 per million. That is about 44 times cheaper than Sonnet, a 98% reduction.

These are published list prices. They leave out the Lambda, which also runs for less time per ticket now.

One thing that surprised us was that JSON key order changed the answer. Sending the same content with keys in a different order moved the output probabilities by up to 0.19. We now send every request with sorted keys, so if you serve a decision model behind an API, check this before you compare runs.

Our lessons

This worked because the task is a closed choice from a known catalog, the volume is high, and the latency of the old path mattered. If your labels need explanation text, if the catalog changes weekly, or if you can’t fit the useful context into a few thousand tokens, a decision model probably can’t replace the LLM’s job.

The part we’d copy regardless of model is the three-way switch. Running both on real traffic, then judging every disagreement, told us more than any offline eval would have. It also meant going back was a 45-second config change.

The world of agents gets a lot more exciting (and less costly) with decision models. If you’re running a classification agent, try the Strands Decider repo and its serving notes.

entry.title: ClickHouse Acquires Xata
entry.content:
Xata is joining ClickHouse

By:

Monica Sarbu

Published:

Reading time:

6 min read

Today, we're excited to announce that Xata is joining ClickHouse to bring agentic capabilities to ClickHouse Managed Postgres.

Together with ClickHouse, we're building a Postgres platform designed for modern applications and AI agents, combining high-performance production workloads on local NVMe storage with Xata’s technology for instant database provisioning, instant copy-on-write branching, and scale-to-zero compute.

Nothing changes for Xata customers in the short term and we continue to accept new sign-ups. In parallel, we're working on bringing branching and an agentic tier to ClickHouse Managed Postgres. We will eventually migrate Xata customers to ClickHouse Managed Postgres. You can also read ClickHouse's announcement.

What is Xata

It’s undeniable that this year software development has changed forever, with agents and software factories now doing the grunt work. However, the increase in coding output has uncovered new bottlenecks. For many companies the database workflows are now the bottleneck: every pull request and every agent run needs a safe, isolated database with production-like data.

Traditionally, creating a copy of a production database is a slow and expensive process, especially when dealing with terabytes of data. Creating a database for every pull request or agent run simply doesn't scale with traditional cloning. With copy-on-write branching, however, there's no need to copy the data, making it possible to create a new branch with production data in seconds.

This is exactly what we’ve built at Xata. Even if a database has multiple terabytes of data, creating a branch takes only around 3 seconds. This means the schema and the data appear as if they were instantly copied to the child branch. At the same time, the child branch is fully independent: it has its own compute, running on a different physical node, and nothing that happens on the child branch impacts the parent database.

The key capabilities are:

Instant database provisioning: Create a new, fully functional Postgres database instantly.Instant copy-on-write branching: Create database branches in seconds, without duplicating the underlying data. You only pay for the diff: create 50 branches of a 1TB database and you’re billed for something much closer to 1TB than 50TB.Scale-to-zero compute: Automatically suspend idle databases and wake them on the next connection, in about one second, minimizing costs.Anonymized production data: Remove sensitive information before data leaves production, so developers and agents can safely work with database branches.

Together, these capabilities make it remarkably cheap to run a branch per PR, per agent run, or even per SQL session. AI-native customers like Sapien, Enginy, David AI, Runner AI, and LoopAI each create thousands of database branches every week.

You might also know Xata from our open-source projects in the Postgres ecosystem, including pgstream, for logical replication with anonymization and DDL support, and pgroll, for zero-downtime, reversible schema changes.

Why ClickHouse

Earlier this year, ClickHouse launched ClickHouse Managed Postgres, which became generally available today. Built on local NVMe storage, it's currently the fastest Postgres service out there, and not by a small margin.

When we started talking with the ClickHouse Managed Postgres team, it quickly became clear just how complementary the two services are: ClickHouse Managed Postgres is optimized for high-throughput, long-lived production workloads, while Xata is designed to provision large numbers of small, short-lived databases in seconds, with production-like data and capabilities like instant branching and scale-to-zero that are particularly well suited for agentic workloads.

Both platforms run unmodified vanilla Postgres and share a strong focus on reliability and stability. The common foundation puts us in a great position to move quickly on integrating the two platforms. In fact, David AI is an example of a customer that already uses ClickHouse Managed Postgres and Xata together and they shared the following with us:

As an AI company working with large volumes of data, we need reliable infrastructure that help us move fast. We moved from Neon to ClickHouse Managed Postgres for better reliability and performance, and our users immediately noticed how much faster everything felt. Xata’s branching has been a great fit for our devs (and AI coding agents!), making it easy to build and test in parallel. Bringing both together means high-performance Postgres and instant branching in a single platform, simplifying our infrastructure and giving our team more time to build.

Best-in-class OLTP and OLAP

By almost any measure, Postgres is the most popular OLTP database and ClickHouse is the most popular OLAP database. Combining the two is something teams have been stitching together themselves for years. The Postgres team at ClickHouse has been making that integration first-class: very fast replication from Postgres into ClickHouse and a unified query layer to build applications.

An integrated transactional and analytical data platform is something we've wanted to build since Xata's early days, when our first product paired Postgres with a search and analytics engine.

On a personal level, we've long admired ClickHouse and already knew the founders and many of the engineers, which gives us confidence that together we can take this vision much further.

What Xata enablesA database branch for every pull request and agent run

The GitHub integration enables automatically creating an isolated database branch for every pull request. These branches can be integrated into CI/CD pipelines, allowing code changes to be safely tested before merging into production. Since they are only needed for testing, branches are often scaling to zero after only a few minutes, minimizing costs.

The same approach applies to coding agents, where every agent run can have its own isolated database to develop and test changes without affecting production.

For details on the branch-per-PR use case and the cost savings it provides, see this blog post.

Powering AI platforms

AI platforms that embed Postgres are seeing an explosion in demand: first thousands, then hundreds of thousands, and eventually millions of databases per week. There are two main use cases: instant database provisioning for every new application, and a database branch for every deployment preview, allowing code changes to be tested safely against production data.

Because unused databases scale to zero, platforms can run very large fleets of small, mostly idle databases at a fraction of the cost, while keeping full compatibility, since it's simply vanilla Postgres.

How it works

Two key technologies enable fast branching and short wake-up times: our Xatastor storage engine and warm pools for compute instances.

Xatastor is our storage engine, which provides separation of storage and compute, high multi-tenancy, copy-on-write branching, compression, thin provisioning, and more. It exposes ZFS zvols over the network using the NVMe/TCP protocol. Because it works at the block-device level, we can run unmodified vanilla PostgreSQL. For a deep-dive into the Xatastor architecture, see this dedicated blog post.

We use warm pools of compute instances to obtain super fast provisioning, wake-up after scale-to-zero, and branching times. This removes the actual node and pod provisioning from the hot path of making a new database or branch available. You can find more information about how this works in this blog post.

What's next

Building Xata has been an incredible journey over the last five years. We're extremely proud of the technology we've built, and even more proud of the team behind it, which is now joining ClickHouse.

We've tackled some really difficult engineering challenges, and it's been incredibly rewarding to see developers and customers embrace these capabilities, creating exponentially more branches as they expand their usage.

What excites us most about this next chapter is that the vision behind Xata is more relevant than ever, and as part of ClickHouse, we're in the best possible position to bring it to fruition.

What this means for you:

If you're a Xata customer: you can continue using it as usual. We'll integrate Xata's features into ClickHouse Managed Postgres, and once there's feature parity, we'll migrate customers as smoothly as possible, ideally with no impact on the service.If you're a ClickHouse Managed Postgres customer: branching, scale-to-zero and an agentic tier are coming to ClickHouse Managed PostgresIf you're new to both: you can get started with ClickHouse Managed Postgres or sign up for Xata today.

We're excited about what we can build together with ClickHouse, and this is just the beginning.

Fireworks AI security breach impacts Notion and their customers
entry.content:
Notice about the Fireworks AI incident that may impact some Notion workspaces

This notice is about the security incident at one of our vendors, Fireworks AI, that may impact some Notion workspaces. For the latest on the Fireworks AI incident, see their official security updates here.

Following an investigation by the Notion security team, we have determined that <1% of Notion workspaces may have been affected by the Fireworks security incident. Some unattributable chat sessions with Notion AI may have been exposed in this incident. “Unattributable” means the chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts did not contain tool call results. Beyond what’s in the chat transcript itself, there’s no information tying the chat back to a workspace, user, or company. No other data from within the workspace is affected.

What is Fireworks AI and how we used them

Fireworks is one of the most-used global AI infrastructure platforms powering tens of thousands of customers, and used by hundreds of thousands of developers. We used Fireworks for classification jobs to help customers understand their own AI usage through a feature in Notion called Insights, and we used them as a general inference provider to serve open-weight models inside our product. The Insights feature has been disabled as we investigate this incident, and we are no longer serving open-weight models through Fireworks.

What happened and how we addressed it

We learned from Fireworks about potential incidents earlier this month, and we shut down all connections to their systems out of an abundance of caution.

On November 6, Fireworks notified us that malicious actors may have accessed potential customer data. Our team immediately began another internal investigation. On November 8, Fireworks confirmed this new dataset for us.

Upon analysis of the new data, we discovered that it included unattributable Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature. Chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts did not contain any tool call results. Beyond the words in the chat transcripts themselves, the data contained no information that could specifically identify the workspace, user, or company.

No other Notion data from your workspace is affected, and we continue to monitor this incident.

If neither you nor your workspace owner has heard from us, that means your workspace is not affected, and no action is needed right now.

For the workspaces impacted by the Fireworks AI incident (<1% of the Notion workspaces), we have contacted the workspace owners. Affected customers will be able to retrieve and review the affected data securely inside their workspace.

For the workspaces affected by the Fireworks AI incident, workspace owners can view the affected data by going to their workspace sidebar → ? → Security incident review. To view this data, use the desktop app or a web browser and make sure you’re on the latest version of Notion. This data is not accessible on mobile.

Workspace owners on Enterprise plans can access:

A CSV of your workspace’s data affected by the incident. Only workspace owners can see this data.

An annotated CSV of the same affected workspace data with additional metadata, such as the user associated with each chat transcript, to help you understand and run your own analysis of the impact. These added annotations and metadata were not exposed as part of the incident. Additional annotated fields are marked with __metadata or __analysis respectively. Only workspace owners can see this data.

Note: These resources are only available if you have managed members for your workspace. Reach out to your account team if you have questions.

 Workspace owners on all other plan types can access:

A page that includes a link they can share with affected members to review their own data.

 For other workspace roles:

Workspace owners can provide a link to members so members can see their own affected data.

Once shared, the link will provide members with a CSV of only the member's own data affected by the incident.

We recommend that you treat this data as if it were exposed. If you or anyone on your team pasted sensitive information like passwords, API keys, or other credentials into Notion AI during this timeframe, we recommend rotating them right away.

FAQs

What is Fireworks and how did Notion use them?

Fireworks AI is one of the most used global AI infrastructure platforms powering tens of thousands of customers and used by hundreds of thousands of developers.

As of November 3rd, we have disconnected our systems from Fireworks, deleted all data in the Fireworks system, and stopped sending all data and traffic to Fireworks. We have also halted all training runs.

We previously used Fireworks for classification jobs to help customers understand their own AI usage through a feature in Notion called Insights and as a general inference provider to serve open-weight models inside our product.

What does “unattributable” mean? Could the conversations still contain sensitive information?

Following an investigation by the Notion security team, we have determined that <1% of Notion workspaces may have been affected by the Fireworks security incident. Some unattributable chat sessions with Notion AI may have been exposed.

"Unattributable" means the chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from. The transcripts also did not contain tool call results (e.g., Notion page content, or external data pulled in by Notion AI.) Beyond what’s in the chat transcript itself, there’s no information tying the chat back to specific workspaces, users, or companies. No other data from within your workspace is affected.

As a precaution, we recommend that you treat this unattributable data as if it were exposed. If anyone on your team pasted sensitive information like passwords, API keys, or other credentials into Notion AI during this timeframe, we recommend rotating them right away.

How did Notion use Fireworks with the Learning and Early Access Program (LEAP)?

Customers in the Learning and Early Access Program (LEAP) volunteer their data to help Notion test new AI technology. In the past, we used this volunteered data to experiment with training task-specific models on Fireworks.

Where can I learn more about Notion’s security practices?

Visit our Security page for an overview of Notion’s security and privacy practices. For more information on security policies, security audit reports, penetration test results, and additional resources, visit the Notion Trust Center.

entry.title: M John Harrison becomes first science fiction author to win the Booker prize
entry.content:
Eighty-one-year-old M John Harrison has won the Booker prize for The End of Everything, a postapocalyptic novel set on a near-future Kent coast, becoming the oldest winner in the award’s history.

Gaby Wood, chief executive of the Booker Prize Foundation, said that while plenty of previous winners had dabbled in science fiction, Harrison’s was “the first Booker winner to have emerged from the bona fide SF world”. She called it “a historic win, for a writer whose decades of work are lightly worn on every page”.

Harrison, who has been publishing for six decades, overtakes Margaret Atwood, who was 79 when she shared the prize in 2019 for The Testaments. He received the £50,000 award and trophy at a ceremony in London on Monday evening.

The End of Everything, Harrison’s first Booker nomination, is set a few decades from now, years after a disaster nobody can properly account for. Set on the Kent coast, the novel sees Phillip Tennent and his ageing aunt Marnie attempting to survive alongside the looming threat of the mysterious iGhetti: vast, shape-changing beings whose origins and intentions are never explained. At 198 pages, it was the shortest book on the shortlist.

Mary Beard, chair of the judges, said the decision was unanimous, reached after a full day of discussion. “It’s a book that turns you upside down, raises a wry smile – and surprisingly, given the subject matter, leaves you with a twinge of optimism,” she said. “One main point of the book is that if, or when, such an apocalypse comes it will be incomprehensible. And the old rules won’t matter either … This is the politics of now seen through the lens of the future.”

Harrison, born in Rugby, Warwickshire, in 1945, sold his first story in 1965 and spent most of the 1970s running the books pages of the speculative fiction magazine New Worlds. Alongside his novels he has written five short-story collections and the “anti-memoir” Wish I Was Here (2023). Climbers took the Boardman Tasker prize for mountain literature in 1989, Nova Swing the Arthur C Clarke award in 2007, and The Sunken Land Begins to Rise Again the Goldsmiths prize in 2020. Once a keen climber and fell runner, he sat on the Booker judging panel in 2022.

This year’s shortlist included two former winners: Marlon James, the bookmakers’ favourite, for The Disappearers, and Douglas Stuart for John of John. Elizabeth Strout’s The Things We Never Say, Luke Kennard’s Black Bag and Rebecca Perry’s debut May We Feed the King completed the list. Each shortlisted author receives £2,500.

Writing in the Guardian on his inspiration last week, Harrison described The End of Everything as “a disaster story in which the disaster is the failure to comprehend”, with aliens who arrive “as incomers from another dimension, paralleling the gentrification of places like the UK’s south-east coast”. He admitted to passing on to the reader “some of the puzzlement and confusion of the characters”, but said he hoped the issues were transparent – among them “the collapse of rationality that comes with Trumpism and the internet”.

His win marks a rare moment of mainstream recognition for a writer long revered by his peers but at the margins of literary fiction. On BBC Radio 4’s Front Row last month, Harrison said he had been “working for 40 to 50 years to shift the balance, both as a novelist and as a critic”, adding: “Why shouldn’t a well written [work of] SF be considered to be literary fiction?”

Even admirers concede the book is not an easy read. In a rave review for the Guardian, Michel Faber said it “exposes the terrifying insecurity of life right now”, but warned that “it won’t be for everyone”.

The win is timely in the age of AI. Beard noted that the “i” in iGhetti hints “at something digital, but you can’t be sure”, while Wood described the book’s post-apocalyptic landscape as “Large Language Model-dotted”.

The judging panel also included Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker, authors Patricia Lockwood and Raymond Antrobus and Guardian journalist Rebecca Liu. They considered 163 books published in the UK or Ireland between 1 October 2025 and 30 September 2026.

It is the first Booker win for Serpent’s Tail, an imprint of the independent publisher Profile Books, and its fifth nomination. Hungarian-British author David Szalay won last year with Flesh; other recent winners include Samantha Harvey’s Orbital, Paul Lynch’s Prophet Song and Shehan Karunatilaka’s The Seven Moons of Maali Almeida.

The End of Everything by M. John Harrison (Profile, £16.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.
